# Literature Review {#sec-lit-review}

This chapter reviews the methodological foundations that motivate the rest of the thesis, beginning with the design and analysis of cluster-randomized trials and then turning to related topics such as the intraclass correlation coefficient, missing data, and multiple imputation.

## Cluster Randomized Trials {#sec-crt}

In health and social science research, studies often randomize entire pre-existing groups---such as clinics, schools, or communities---instead of single individuals. As @lorenzClusterRandomizedStudies2018a and @murrayEssentialIngredientsInnovations2020 explain, this approach is essential when an intervention naturally targets a whole environment or to prevent "contamination," which occurs when control group members accidentally adopt aspects of the treatment from their peers. These studies can take several structural forms, including classic CRTs, stepped-wedge designs (where groups cross over to the intervention sequentially over time), and partially clustered trials (where individuals are randomized independently but receive treatment in group settings). Regardless of the specific design, grouping participants fundamentally changes how we view statistical data: people in the same cluster share identical staff, environments, and policies, making their outcomes naturally more alike. While statistical models can account for this group structure, they cannot eliminate or mitigate the underlying lack of independence among individuals---it remains an inherent feature of the data.

To measure this group similarity, researchers calculate the intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC). The ICC is then used to determine the "design effect," a scaling formula that illustrates how the impact of correlation is strongly magnified by cluster sample size. Accounting for the design effect is essential in both the planning and analysis phases of a study: failing to use it during sample size design leads to underpowered trials and high Type II error rates (false negatives), while ignoring it during final analysis understates uncertainty and inflates Type I error rates (false positives).

Specifically, because outcomes within groups are linked, analyzing cluster-randomized trials (CRTs) requires statistical models that directly account for this correlation structure. @murrayEssentialIngredientsInnovations2020 trace how analytical methods have evolved over time---moving from simple cluster-level summaries to individual-level approaches like linear mixed models and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE). They emphasize that no single analysis method is universally superior because each involves distinct statistical trade-offs. For instance, @murrayEssentialIngredientsInnovations2020 note that while collapsing data into a single cluster summary score is simple and avoids complex statistical modeling, it cannot easily adjust for individual participant traits (like age or baseline health status). Building smoothly on these analytical choices, @billotHowShouldCluster2024 explain why individual-level regression methods are generally preferred in trial practice. Beyond allowing researchers to adjust for baseline participant traits to improve estimation precision, individual-level mixed-effects models explicitly separate between-cluster variance from within-cluster variance, providing the exact model components needed to calculate the ICC directly.

However, analyzing CRTs becomes significantly more complex when trials face real-world complications like missing data and small sample sizes. @billotHowShouldCluster2024 point out that simply accounting for clustering in a model does not solve the challenge of missing participant outcomes, which requires deliberate imputation strategies. Compounding this difficulty, @kahanIncreasedRiskType2016 demonstrate that standard, uncorrected mixed models and GEE tend to underestimate standard errors when cluster counts are low (frequently under 30 to 70 clusters). This distortion creates a high risk of Type I errors---or false positives---tricking researchers into declaring a treatment effective when it is not, with false-positive rates often soaring far above the standard 5% target. To prevent misleading conclusions, @kahanIncreasedRiskType2016 highlight the necessity of applying small-sample corrections (such as Satterthwaite degree-of-freedom adjustments or Fay-Graubard variance corrections) to restore proper standard errors.

Together, these foundational articles reveal how clustering affects every stage of research, from initial sample size planning to final statistical modeling. Ignoring intra-cluster correlation artificially inflates statistical power and understates uncertainty. Understanding these basic CRT mechanics provides a strong foundation for exploring how downstream complications---specifically missing data and ICC estimation---must be handled without destroying the underlying group structure.
